Textbook

Prerequisites
Python, linear algebra, basic calculus, and introductory probability


Format
A 16-week semester or a 10-week quarter, with two 75-minute lectures per week


Materials
Slides · Labs · TinyTorch (instructor guide for autograding) · no GPUs needed

title: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems
text:
Description
Students study how data pipelines, training, optimization, and deployment work on a single machine with up to eight accelerators. Along the way they build a small deep learning framework, TinyTorch, one module at a time.

title: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems
text:
Learning outcomes
By the end of the course, students can:

Build a small deep learning framework that trains a model.
Measure where time and memory go in a training or inference workload.
Choose optimizations, such as compression, against deployment constraints.
Deploy and evaluate a model against latency, memory, and quality targets.

Courses

Introduction to Machine Learning Systems






Volume I · Semester plan
Students study data pipelines, training, optimization, and deployment on a single machine, and they build their own framework with TinyTorch.
Requires: a laptop. The labs run in a browser, so no GPU is needed.
Course · Syllabus · Slides · Labs · TinyTorch





Scaling Machine Learning Systems






Volume II · Semester plan
Students study distributed training, communication, fault recovery, and serving across many machines, and they finish with a design project.
Requires: a laptop. The labs simulate the cluster, so no GPU is needed.
Course · Syllabus · Slides · Labs





Edge AI






Volume I · Learning path
Students deploy models on Linux edge devices, reading Volume I alongside the Raspberry Pi kit and its companion book.
Requires: one Raspberry Pi per student or team, from about $60 for a Raspberry Pi 5. The reading list gives the options.
Course · Reading list · Slides · Hardware kits





TinyML






Volume I · Historical materials
Students train models and deploy them on microcontrollers. The materials come from earlier Harvard offerings, with their assignments and example projects.
Requires: one microcontroller board per student or team, from about $25. The syllabus lists the options and prices.

title: Scaling Machine Learning Systems
text:
Description
Students study how distributed training, communication, fault recovery, and serving work across many machines. The course ends with a design project that students defend in a written report.

title: Scaling Machine Learning Systems
text:
Learning outcomes
By the end of the course, students can:

Choose a parallelism strategy for a training workload and justify it with measurements.
Explain how a training job recovers its progress after failures.
Size a serving system for a stated demand, cost, and energy budget.
Defend a fleet design in a written report.

title: TinyML
text:
Description
Students train machine learning models and deploy them on microcontrollers, where memory, energy, and latency are tightly limited. The course moves from fundamentals to applications and then to deployment on real hardware. Part IV, on MLOps, is optional.

title: TinyML
text:
Learning outcomes
By the end of the course, students can:

Train and quantize a model small enough for a microcontroller.
Deploy keyword spotting, visual wake words, and gesture recognition on a board.
Collect a custom dataset and build an end-to-end TinyML application.
